questions.prompt: An agent rewrote a function and renamed it in the file, but three other files still call the old name and now fail to build. Which tool is designed for exactly this?
options: `git diff` followed by manual edits in each file
Rename-everywhere (F2 in VS Code), which updates every reference structurally
A global find-and-replace across the project
`git stash pop` to undo the rename
questions.explanation: Rename-everywhere understands scope — it changes the declaration and each reference, and it won't touch a same-named string or a different symbol. Find-and-replace changes text, so it will happily corrupt something that merely looks identical.

questions.prompt: An agent's change touches 14 files and you can't tell if 3 of them are wrong. What is the fastest honest way to judge it?
options: Open all 14 files and read them in the editor
`git diff --stat` first to see the shape, then `git diff` per suspicious file
`git stash push` it and ask the agent to redo it
`git log --oneline` to see whether it committed anything
questions.explanation: `--stat` shows how many lines moved per file in one screen — that tells you where the risk is before you read a single line of content. Then narrow to the files that look wrong. Option A works but scales badly; option D answers a question you didn't ask.

questions.prompt: Why does this lesson teach `git stash push` instead of `git checkout -- file` for rejecting an agent's bad edit?
options: `checkout` deletes the change permanently; the stash keeps it recoverable so you can still read what the agent tried
`checkout` cannot restore a single file in a repo with commits
`stash` also commits the change to the branch
questions.explanation: `git checkout -- file` throws the working-tree version away — including the good half of an edit you might want. The stash is a commit off-branch: your file returns to its committed state and nothing is lost. You can read it with `git stash show -p stash@{0}` and bring it back with `git stash pop`.
